summary: Explains that a BGP speaker applying policy based on the RPKI should not send route refresh requests to neighbors just because it got new RPKI data. It describes how to avoid that by keeping a full Adj-RIB-In or saving paths dropped by route origin validation. It updates RFC 8481. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When new rules arrive, a router should not ask everyone to resend everything. It should keep the rejected routes on a shelf so it can check them again.

subtitle: BGP routers doing RPKI checks should keep the routes they drop instead of asking neighbors to resend everything.

tldr.problem: Some BGP speakers that perform RPKI-based policy do not keep paths they marked Invalid, so when new RPKI data arrives they send route refresh requests to all peers, which burdens those peers.
tldr.mechanism: The speaker keeps a full Adj-RIB-In, or at least the routes dropped due to ROV, so it can reevaluate them against new RPKI data with no route refresh. A global operator control enables the saving.
tldr.outcome: Keeping dropped routes becomes a mandatory capability for BGP speakers performing ROV. The RFC updates RFC 8481.

today: RFC 9324 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2022 that updates RFC 8481. It has not been obsoleted or updated itself.

sections.title: The Route Refresh Problem
sections.content:
Early BGP speakers had memory limits, so classic implementations did not keep a full Adj-RIB-In. When such a speaker does RPKI-based Route Origin Validation (ROV) and receives new RPKI data, it may no longer hold the paths it earlier marked Invalid. It must then request a route refresh from its neighbors to recover paths that the new data may cover.

Neighbors perceive this as rude, because it passes a serious resource burden on to them. RFC 9324 recommends that implementations keep and mark paths affected by RPKI-based policy, so route refresh is no longer needed.
sections.eli5: If a router threw away some routes and later needs them back, it has to ask all its neighbors to resend them. That is a lot of work for the neighbors.

sections.title: What Went Wrong in Practice
sections.content:
As ROV dropping Invalids has deployed, some BGP speaker implementations were found to issue a route refresh to all sending peers whenever they received new Validated ROA Payloads (VRPs). The RFC reports that this was very destructive. In reaction, ROV has been turned off in some places, and there have been actual de-peerings.

The problem grows with RPKI registration and ROA creation, on the order of the in-degree of ROV-implementing BGP speakers. It is expected to grow further as Autonomous System Provider Authorization (ASPA) is used. Other mechanisms with similar flux rates, such as automated policy provisioning, could cause similar problems. For this reason the document updates RFC 8481.
sections.eli5: Some operators got so many resend requests that they switched their route checking off, or even stopped connecting with the sender.

sections.title: Keeping Partial Adj-RIB-In Data
sections.content:
A route dropped by operator policy due to ROV is considered ineligible to compete for the best route, but it MUST be kept in the Adj-RIB-In for potential future evaluation. A full Adj-RIB-In can be a problem for resource-constrained speakers, so the RFC allows keeping less: an implementation that does not retain the full Adj-RIB-In MUST retain at least the routes dropped due to ROV.

Because storing these routes may strain small devices, there MUST be a global operation, CLI, YANG or other mechanism that lets the operator enable the feature. The control MUST NOT be per peer, since that could cause inconsistent behavior.

Policy that may drop routes due to RPKI-based checks (ROV, and in future ASPA, BGPsec and so on) MUST run, and the dropped routes MUST be saved, before non-RPKI policies run, because those may change path attributes.
sections.eli5: The router must keep the routes it rejected, at least, in a drawer. The owner turns the drawer on or off for the whole router, not one neighbor at a time.

sections.title: Operational Recommendations
sections.content:
Operators deploying ROV or other RPKI-based policy should make sure their BGP speaker does not cause route refresh requests to neighbors. BGP speakers MUST either keep the full Adj-RIB-In or implement the behavior above; this is an additional, mandatory capability for speakers performing ROV.

If the speaker lacks the feature, the operator should enable the vendor's control for keeping the full Adj-RIB-In, sometimes called "soft reconfiguration inbound", and measure that no unnecessary refresh requests are sent. Equipment with too few resources for either option SHOULD be replaced or SHOULD NOT be used for ROV.

A misconfigured neighbor might send a massive number of paths and consume a lot of memory, so pre-policy filtering such as that in an Internet-Draft on inbound maximum prefix limits could reduce the exposure. Route refresh toward more than one peer can cause churn in best route selection and outbound signaling. Internet Exchange Points running route servers (RFC 7947) should watch for members, or their own speakers, causing excessive route refresh load.
sections.eli5: Owners should check their routers are not nagging neighbors. If a router is too small to keep the extra routes, it is better to upgrade it or not use route checking on it.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The document describes a denial of service that ROV or other RPKI policy may place on a BGP neighbor and how to ameliorate it. Otherwise it adds no security considerations beyond those of the documents it references. It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The main danger here is a router accidentally overloading its neighbors, and this document explains how to avoid that.
